planting.note: Transplant young plants or divisions in early-to-mid spring once the ground has thawed, siting crowns slightly above grade in a crevice or scree bed so excess moisture never pools around the base.

directions: Heuchera alba, the white alumroot, occupies dry, south-facing shale and sandstone ledges and barrens from Pennsylvania and Maryland south through the Virginias and into the southern Appalachians, rooting into thin crevice soil above bare rock. Unlike the pink- or red-flowered alumroots grown as garden ornamentals, this species sends up airy, open panicles of small greenish-white to cream flowers well above low mounds of lobed, mottled leaves in late spring. In cultivation it wants the same sharp drainage it finds on its native scree, a crevice garden, dry wall, or gritty raised bed in full sun to light shade, and resents heavy, moisture-retentive soils that cause crown rot. It has long been grown by rock-garden and native-plant enthusiasts both as a garden subject in its own right and as breeding stock for white-flowered Heuchera selections.
sources: Weakley's Flora of the Southeastern United States

planting.note: Fall-sow seed directly onto bare, lean, rocky soil so it can overwinter and cold-stratify naturally, or set out spring divisions into a well-drained scree slope.

directions: Harris's goldenrod is a narrow endemic of loose, actively eroding shale talus and barren slopes in Virginia, West Virginia, Maryland, and Pennsylvania, forming low clumps with narrower, more sharply toothed leaves and a flatter-topped flower cluster than its widespread relative Solidago arguta, with which it is sometimes merged taxonomically. Plants root deeply into the shifting shale scree to reach moisture far below the parched surface, an adaptation that also makes them remarkably drought tolerant in an ordinary garden setting. Late-summer sprays of small bright-yellow flowers draw a long list of native bees, wasps, and migrating butterflies. Grow it in lean, fast-draining, rocky soil in full sun; rich garden beds produce lax, floppy growth that loses the tight, wind-adapted habit seen on its home barrens.
sources: Weakley's Flora of the Southeastern United States
Virginia Native Plant Society seed exchange

planting.note: Nick or sand the hard seed coat and direct-sow in early spring into lean, rocky soil, since milkvetches resent root disturbance and transplant poorly once established.

directions: This shale-barren race of bent milkvetch is restricted to the loose, droughty scree of Devonian shale slopes in Virginia and West Virginia, distinguished from the more widespread limestone-glade form of Astragalus distortus by its habitat and generally more compact, tightly clustered growth. Low mounds of pinnate, silvery-haired foliage send up short racemes of pale lavender pea flowers in mid-spring, followed by distinctively twisted, bladdery seedpods that give the species its name. Like most milkvetches it carries nitrogen-fixing root nodules and performs best in lean, mineral soil with no supplemental fertilizer, since rich conditions encourage disease-prone, overly lush growth. Set plants in full sun on a steep, gravelly slope or scree bed that drains instantly after rain.
sources: Platt, R.B. (1951) Ecological Monographs — shale barren flora study

planting.note: Plant bulbs or direct-sow fresh seed in fall into a gritty, fast-draining scree bed, mimicking the loose shale chips of its native barrens.

directions: The shale-barren wild onion is one of the true shale-barren endemics catalogued by shale-barren specialist Edgar T. Wherry, found only on a scatter of open, scree-covered Devonian shale slopes in West Virginia and adjacent Virginia. It forms small clumps of narrow, sharply pointed leaves topped in summer by compact, pale pink to white nodding umbels on wiry stems, closely resembling a dwarfed version of the far more common nodding onion. Bulbs need the same combination of baking summer heat, bone-dry surface soil, and cool, moisture-holding rock below that defines the shale-barren microclimate, so a steep scree bed or crevice planting with a thin gravel mulch gives the best results. Because wild populations are small and scattered, garden stock has historically circulated mainly through rock-garden society seed exchanges rather than commercial channels.
sources: Wherry, E.T. — shale barren flora studies
North American Rock Garden Society seed exchange

planting.note: Divide and transplant clumps in early spring into lean, gritty soil, spacing plants to allow the tufted foliage to fill in without crowding.

directions: Parasol sedge is a tufted, fine-textured sedge of dry, open, sun-baked barrens and rocky woodland edges across much of eastern North America, reaching some of its best, most compact growth on the thin, well-drained shale scree of Appalachian barrens where competing vegetation is sparse. Its short, wiry, semi-evergreen leaves form dense, grass-like tussocks only a few inches tall, with inconspicuous flower spikes held low among the foliage in spring. It tolerates both drought and poor, mineral soil far better than most ornamental sedges, making it a useful small-scale groundcover for a gravel garden, dry rock garden, or barren-themed planting. Set divisions into lean, sharply drained soil in full sun to very light shade.

planting.note: Direct-sow in early spring onto bare, lean soil or scatter seed over gravel mulch, since this bluet germinates and self-sows best on open, disturbed mineral ground.

directions: This shale-barren variety of purple bluet, or Venus' pride, is distinguished from the widespread woodland form by noticeably larger, more conspicuous calyx lobes that persist around the seed capsule, a trait documented from open shale-barren populations in the Ridge and Valley of Virginia and West Virginia. Clusters of small, funnel-shaped lavender-pink flowers with a darker throat open over a low mat of oval leaves from late spring into summer, drawing small bees and butterflies to an otherwise sparsely vegetated, sun-scorched slope. It is considerably more drought tolerant than typical woodland bluets and resents the rich, consistently moist soil that suits most garden wildflowers. Grow it in lean, gritty, well-drained soil in full sun, and allow it to self-sow along gravel paths or scree edges the way it colonizes bare shale float in the wild.
sources: Weakley's Flora of the Southeastern United States

subcategory: native rock outcrop shale cliff perennial

planting.note: Direct-sow in fall into vertical rock crevices or a tufa/scree bed so winter cold stratifies the seed naturally before spring germination.

directions: Branched draba is a small, cushion-forming mustard of dry Appalachian cliffs and rock ledges from Pennsylvania to Alabama, most frequent on calcareous rock but also documented on shale and sandstone outcrops, including barren margins in the central Appalachians. In spring, wiry, much-branched stems covered in tiny star-shaped hairs rise from a tight basal rosette and carry open sprays of small, four-petaled yellow flowers, followed by flattened, twisted seedpods that give the plant a wispy, airy look. It is a true crevice plant, rooting into narrow rock cracks with almost no soil and needing the same bone-dry, alkaline-to-neutral, sharply draining conditions in cultivation, a tufa wall, crevice garden, or gritty scree bed in full sun suits it best. It has a long history in specialist rock-garden cultivation and periodically appears in alpine and rock-garden society seed exchanges.
sources: North American Rock Garden Society seed exchange
